trial.ground_truth: Inventory executes pg_sleep(1.2) before catalog SQL
trial.predicted_root_cause: inventory-service's request path issues SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) against Postgres, adding a deterministic ~1.2s wait to every affected request. Postgres active sessions attribute the PgSleep/Timeout waits to application_name "inventory-service", and inventory-service's db_qps rises ~20x over baseline (0.18 -> 3.96) while every other service's db_qps decreases. The resulting ~1.2s server-side delay propagates upward: order-service /checkout (p50 ~1234ms) waits on its inventory dependency (critical-path span 997066ac7daecce5 GET 1212ms inside order-service POST /checkout 1233ms), and gateway (p50 ~1246ms) waits on order-service. error_pct is 0.00 in every service, so this is a latency injection, not a failure or exception. The /products ORDER BY id list query itself is fast (call deltas are normal); the pg_sleep statement is the specific added delay, so a single code path introduces the latency rather than DB resource contention or pool exhaustion.

regression_risks: Remediation was operational (terminate sessions / remove pg_sleep) with no code location identified, so the artificial delay could recur if the source statement is not located and removed.
If a legitimate slow query later recurs, raising pool_max as a mitigation may mask the root cause and increase DB load.
Alerting/allowlist changes (pg_sleep detection, db_qps relative-change) are recommendations only and not evidenced as implemented.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Sufficient for diagnosis: three independent DB snapshots, cross-service metrics isolating inventory-service, health ruling out pool exhaustion, and a measured before/after showing p50 recovery (gateway 1243->31.5ms, inventory 1207->2.6ms). Insufficient to verify a production deployment or the code location of the pg_sleep statement, which was not found in scope.
critic_result.verification_summary: Diagnosis of DATABASE_SLOW_QUERY via an injected SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) in inventory-service is corroborated by independent, mutually consistent evidence. Three separate inspect_database snapshots (E-9cd00575a0204f82 11:15:08, E-0c85414c130948f2 11:15:30, E-9c0098bc295a4591 11:15:44) each show active sessions executing SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event PgSleep/Timeout attributed to application_name=inventory-service, with per-second pg_sleep call_deltas (3/3/1) matching the request rate. E-6346e6e735ef4a04 shows inventory db_qps anomaly_score ~20.6 (0.18->3.93) with matching p50 ~1207ms while every other service's db_qps decreases and their p50s remain single-digit, isolating the delay to inventory-service. Zero error_pct everywhere supports latency injection over failure. E-4d19d345ad084c9f confirms inventory health 200, pool_available 4/4, requests_waiting 0, ruling out current pool exhaustion. Critically, the requested before/after measurement shows full recovery: gateway p50 1243->31.5ms, inventory 1207->2.6ms, order 1233->30.1ms (E-9419d094b4254251), i.e. after the delay was stopped the cascade cleared. This verifies the causal hypothesis and its tested scope; it does NOT verify any production deployment, and remediation was operational (NO_CODE_PATCH).

arguments.recommended_fix: 1) Immediately confirm and stop the injected delay: run SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE '%pg_sleep%' to identify sessions by application_name, then terminate the offending sessions (SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)) and remove/disable the pg_sleep(1.2) statement from the inventory-service product-lookup code path. 2) Grep the inventory-service codebase outside the current read scope for pg_sleep / sleep / artificial latency injection and remove it or gate it behind a debug flag. 3) After removal, re-measure inventory-service p50 (expect back to double-digit ms) and confirm gateway/order-service p50 drop below ~50ms. 4) Because pool_max=4 with 1.2s-held connections sharply limits inventory throughput, consider raising pool_max only as a mitigation if legitimate slow queries recur. 5) Add a DB statement allowlist/alert on pg_sleep in production and an alert on per-service db_qps relative-change anomaly (the inventory db_qps anomaly_score of ~20 was the clearest early detector).

This is corroborated independently by query_metrics: inventory-service db_qps anomaly_score ~20.6-20.8 (0.18 -> 3.96, increasing) while all other services' db_qps decrease (order 3.65->1.05, payment 3.44->1.11, user 3.96->1.05, notification 3.45->1.07), and inventory p50 ~1207ms matches the 1.2s sleep. Trace 71bbe02c9eee48cfd912330038ef6491 critical path is nested gateway POST /checkout 1248ms -> order-service POST /checkout 1233ms -> span 2233c86daaf56e10 (inventory-service HTTP dependency) and its redis/postgres child spans; the slow portion is the one ~1.2s blocking call, while the other DB/redis spans are single-digit ms. Health: inventory-service HTTP is healthy (200) with available pool 2/4 and requests_waiting 0, so pool exhaustion is not the cause; cumulative_pool requests_errors 16/queued 21/wait_ms 12865 are historical counters, consistent with (not the cause of) 1.2s occupancy of pool connections. Gateway/order/inventory error_pct is 0.00 everywhere, consistent with latency injection and refuting failure/timeout/exception categories. Low request volume (1-2 rps) explains scatter but the ~1.2s p50 in all three services is a persistent deterministic delay, not a throughput artifact. Code search for pg_sleep and inventory service symbols returned no matches within allowed scope (services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py), so the source location cannot be cited; remediation is operational.

E-6346e6e735ef4a04 shows inventory db_qps anomaly_score ~20.6 (0.18->3.93) with matching p50 ~1207ms while every other service's db_qps decreases and their p50s remain single-digit, isolating the delay to inventory-service. Zero error_pct everywhere supports latency injection over failure. E-4d19d345ad084c9f confirms inventory health 200, pool_available 4/4, requests_waiting 0, ruling out current pool exhaustion. Critically, the requested before/after measurement shows full recovery: gateway p50 1243->31.5ms, inventory 1207->2.6ms, order 1233->30.1ms (E-9419d094b4254251), i.e. after the delay was stopped the cascade cleared. This verifies the causal hypothesis and its tested scope; it does NOT verify any production deployment, and remediation was operational (NO_CODE_PATCH).
alternative_explanations: Downstream saturation/throttling rather than pg_sleep: refuted because only inventory-service latency and db_qps spiked while all other services' db_qps decreased and stayed fast; the 1.2s value matches pg_sleep exactly.

Pool exhaustion on inventory-service (pool_max=4): refuted by instantaneous health showing pool_available 4/4 and requests_waiting 0; cumulative counters (errors 16, queued 21, wait_ms 12865) are historical consequences, not current pressure.
Low-volume/measurement artifact: refuted by consistent ~1.2s p50 across repeated windows at higher throughput (1.95 rps) and by the deterministic recovery to single-digit ms after removal.

regression_risks: Remediation was operational (terminate sessions / remove pg_sleep) with no code location identified, so the artificial delay could recur if the source statement is not located and removed.
If a legitimate slow query later recurs, raising pool_max as a mitigation may mask the root cause and increase DB load.
Alerting/allowlist changes (pg_sleep detection, db_qps relative-change) are recommendations only and not evidenced as implemented.

payload.summary: Three independent inspect_database snapshots (11:15:08, 11:15:30, 11:15:44) each show active Postgres sessions running SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event PgSleep/wait_event_type Timeout, attributed to application_name=inventory-service, with pg_sleep call_deltas of 3, 3 and 1 per second sample. This is corroborated independently by query_metrics: inventory-service db_qps anomaly_score ~20.6-20.8 (0.18 -> 3.96, increasing) while all other services' db_qps decrease (order 3.65->1.05, payment 3.44->1.11, user 3.96->1.05, notification 3.45->1.07), and inventory p50 ~1207ms matches the 1.2s sleep. Trace 71bbe02c9eee48cfd912330038ef6491 critical path is nested gateway POST /checkout 1248ms -> order-service POST /checkout 1233ms -> span 2233c86daaf56e10 (inventory-service HTTP dependency) and its redis/postgres child spans; the slow portion is the one ~1.2s blocking call, while the other DB/redis spans are single-digit ms. Health: inventory-service HTTP is healthy (200) with available pool 2/4 and requests_waiting 0, so pool exhaustion is not the cause; cumulative_pool requests_errors 16/queued 21/wait_ms 12865 are historical counters, consistent with (not the cause of) 1.2s occupancy of pool connections. Gateway/order/inventory error_pct is 0.00 everywhere, consistent with latency injection and refuting failure/timeout/exception categories. Low request volume (1-2 rps) explains scatter but the ~1.2s p50 in all three services is a persistent deterministic delay, not a throughput artifact. Code search for pg_sleep and inventory service symbols returned no matches within allowed scope (services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py), so the source location cannot be cited; remediation is operational.

diagnosis.hypothesis: inventory-service executes an artificial slow DB call (SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)) on its /products path, blocking ~1.2s per request and cascading tail latency up through order-service and gateway.
diagnosis.root_cause: inventory-service's request path issues SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) against Postgres, adding a deterministic ~1.2s wait to every affected request. Postgres active sessions attribute the PgSleep/Timeout waits to application_name "inventory-service", and inventory-service's db_qps rises ~20x over baseline (0.18 -> 3.96) while every other service's db_qps decreases. The resulting ~1.2s server-side delay propagates upward: order-service /checkout (p50 ~1234ms) waits on its inventory dependency (critical-path span 997066ac7daecce5 GET 1212ms inside order-service POST /checkout 1233ms), and gateway (p50 ~1246ms) waits on order-service. error_pct is 0.00 in every service, so this is a latency injection, not a failure or exception. The /products ORDER BY id list query itself is fast (call deltas are normal); the pg_sleep statement is the specific added delay, so a single code path introduces the latency rather than DB resource contention or pool exhaustion.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: 1) Immediately confirm and stop the injected delay: run SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE '%pg_sleep%' to identify sessions by application_name, then terminate the offending sessions (SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)) and remove/disable the pg_sleep(1.2) statement from the inventory-service product-lookup code path. 2) Grep the inventory-service codebase outside the current read scope for pg_sleep / sleep / artificial latency injection and remove it or gate it behind a debug flag. 3) After removal, re-measure inventory-service p50 (expect back to double-digit ms) and confirm gateway/order-service p50 drop below ~50ms. 4) Because pool_max=4 with 1.2s-held connections sharply limits inventory throughput, consider raising pool_max only as a mitigation if legitimate slow queries recur. 5) Add a DB statement allowlist/alert on pg_sleep in production and an alert on per-service db_qps relative-change anomaly (the inventory db_qps anomaly_score of ~20 was the clearest early detector).

decision.hypothesis: inventory-service executes an artificial slow DB call (SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)) on its /products path, blocking ~1.2s per request and cascading tail latency up through order-service and gateway.
decision.root_cause: inventory-service's request path issues SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) against Postgres, adding a deterministic ~1.2s wait to every affected request. Postgres active sessions attribute the PgSleep/Timeout waits to application_name "inventory-service", and inventory-service's db_qps rises ~20x over baseline (0.18 -> 3.96) while every other service's db_qps decreases. The resulting ~1.2s server-side delay propagates upward: order-service /checkout (p50 ~1234ms) waits on its inventory dependency (critical-path span 997066ac7daecce5 GET 1212ms inside order-service POST /checkout 1233ms), and gateway (p50 ~1246ms) waits on order-service. error_pct is 0.00 in every service, so this is a latency injection, not a failure or exception. The /products ORDER BY id list query itself is fast (call deltas are normal); the pg_sleep statement is the specific added delay, so a single code path introduces the latency rather than DB resource contention or pool exhaustion.
llm_findings: Three separate inspect_database snapshots (11:15:08/11:15:30/11:15:44) all show active Postgres sessions running SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event_type Timeout attributed to application_name=inventory-service.
Only inventory-service db_qps rises anomalously (~0.18 -> 3.96, anomaly_score ~20.6-20.8) while order/payment/user/notification db_qps all decrease; inventory p50 ~1207ms equals the 1.2s sleep.
Trace 71bbe02c9eee48cfd912330038ef6491 nests gateway 1248ms -> order-service 1233ms -> 1212ms dependency GET; other DB/redis spans in the same trace complete in single-digit ms.
Zero error_pct across gateway, order-service and inventory-service indicates latency injection, refuting failure/timeout/exception categories.

inventory-service /health is 200 with pool_available 2/4 and requests_waiting 0; cumulative pool counters (errors 16, queued 21, wait_ms 12865) are historical and are a consequence of 1.2s-held connections, not the cause.

Code scope (services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py) contains no pg_sleep reference, so no verified code location exists; operational remediation is recommended over a code patch.
decision.recommended_fix: 1) Immediately confirm and stop the injected delay: run SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE '%pg_sleep%' to identify sessions by application_name, then terminate the offending sessions (SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)) and remove/disable the pg_sleep(1.2) statement from the inventory-service product-lookup code path. 2) Grep the inventory-service codebase outside the current read scope for pg_sleep / sleep / artificial latency injection and remove it or gate it behind a debug flag. 3) After removal, re-measure inventory-service p50 (expect back to double-digit ms) and confirm gateway/order-service p50 drop below ~50ms. 4) Because pool_max=4 with 1.2s-held connections sharply limits inventory throughput, consider raising pool_max only as a mitigation if legitimate slow queries recur. 5) Add a DB statement allowlist/alert on pg_sleep in production and an alert on per-service db_qps relative-change anomaly (the inventory db_qps anomaly_score of ~20 was the clearest early detector).
decision.reasoning_summary: Three independent inspect_database snapshots (11:15:08, 11:15:30, 11:15:44) each show active Postgres sessions running SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event PgSleep/wait_event_type Timeout, attributed to application_name=inventory-service, with pg_sleep call_deltas of 3, 3 and 1 per second sample. This is corroborated independently by query_metrics: inventory-service db_qps anomaly_score ~20.6-20.8 (0.18 -> 3.96, increasing) while all other services' db_qps decrease (order 3.65->1.05, payment 3.44->1.11, user 3.96->1.05, notification 3.45->1.07), and inventory p50 ~1207ms matches the 1.2s sleep. Trace 71bbe02c9eee48cfd912330038ef6491 critical path is nested gateway POST /checkout 1248ms -> order-service POST /checkout 1233ms -> span 2233c86daaf56e10 (inventory-service HTTP dependency) and its redis/postgres child spans; the slow portion is the one ~1.2s blocking call, while the other DB/redis spans are single-digit ms. Health: inventory-service HTTP is healthy (200) with available pool 2/4 and requests_waiting 0, so pool exhaustion is not the cause; cumulative_pool requests_errors 16/queued 21/wait_ms 12865 are historical counters, consistent with (not the cause of) 1.2s occupancy of pool connections. Gateway/order/inventory error_pct is 0.00 everywhere, consistent with latency injection and refuting failure/timeout/exception categories. Low request volume (1-2 rps) explains scatter but the ~1.2s p50 in all three services is a persistent deterministic delay, not a throughput artifact. Code search for pg_sleep and inventory service symbols returned no matches within allowed scope (services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py), so the source location cannot be cited; remediation is operational.

deterministic_signals.explanation: gateway p50 ~1246ms with 0% errors; nested critical path shows gateway POST /checkout 1248ms waiting on order-service 1233ms, i.e. gateway is an upstream symptom of a slow downstream dependency, not the origin.

inventory-service p50 ~1207ms matches its own SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) PgSleep/Timeout sessions in Postgres and a ~20x db_qps rise unique to this service; this is the causal origin rather than a pooled-wait symptom (pool available 2/4, waiting 0).

order-service p50 ~1234ms with 0% errors; its /checkout span contains a 1212ms GET dependency call into inventory-service, so order-service is an upstream caller blocked on the same slow inventory path.

remaining_uncertainty: Code location of the pg_sleep(1.2) call could not be identified: search_repository and get_code_symbol returned no matches for pg_sleep / inventory symbols within the allowed scope (services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py), so the patch target is unverified and no CODE_PATCH is proposed.

Trace span 2233c86daaf56e10 is labeled as an inventory-service dependency but its operation name/duration were only partially read; the exact child span carrying the 1.2s wait was inferred from aggregate durations plus DB sessions, not read verbatim.
Whether the pg_sleep is intentional test-load injection vs a regression/fault injected into inventory-service code is not determinable from available evidence.

Cumulative pool counters (requests_errors 16, requests_queued 21, requests_wait_ms 12865) are cumulative and cannot confirm a current separate pool problem; a small independent pool-wait contribution cannot be fully excluded.

regression_risks: Remediation was operational (terminate sessions / remove pg_sleep) with no code location identified, so the artificial delay could recur if the source statement is not located and removed.
If a legitimate slow query later recurs, raising pool_max as a mitigation may mask the root cause and increase DB load.

critic.test_sufficiency: Sufficient for diagnosis: three independent DB snapshots, cross-service metrics isolating inventory-service, health ruling out pool exhaustion, and a measured before/after showing p50 recovery (gateway 1243->31.5ms, inventory 1207->2.6ms). Insufficient to verify a production deployment or the code location of the pg_sleep statement, which was not found in scope.
critic.verification_summary: Diagnosis of DATABASE_SLOW_QUERY via an injected SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) in inventory-service is corroborated by independent, mutually consistent evidence. Three separate inspect_database snapshots (E-9cd00575a0204f82 11:15:08, E-0c85414c130948f2 11:15:30, E-9c0098bc295a4591 11:15:44) each show active sessions executing SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event PgSleep/Timeout attributed to application_name=inventory-service, with per-second pg_sleep call_deltas (3/3/1) matching the request rate. E-6346e6e735ef4a04 shows inventory db_qps anomaly_score ~20.6 (0.18->3.93) with matching p50 ~1207ms while every other service's db_qps decreases and their p50s remain single-digit, isolating the delay to inventory-service. Zero error_pct everywhere supports latency injection over failure. E-4d19d345ad084c9f confirms inventory health 200, pool_available 4/4, requests_waiting 0, ruling out current pool exhaustion. Critically, the requested before/after measurement shows full recovery: gateway p50 1243->31.5ms, inventory 1207->2.6ms, order 1233->30.1ms (E-9419d094b4254251), i.e. after the delay was stopped the cascade cleared. This verifies the causal hypothesis and its tested scope; it does NOT verify any production deployment, and remediation was operational (NO_CODE_PATCH).

alternative_explanations: Downstream saturation/throttling rather than pg_sleep: refuted because only inventory-service latency and db_qps spiked while all other services' db_qps decreased and stayed fast; the 1.2s value matches pg_sleep exactly.

Pool exhaustion on inventory-service (pool_max=4): refuted by instantaneous health showing pool_available 4/4 and requests_waiting 0; cumulative counters (errors 16, queued 21, wait_ms 12865) are historical consequences, not current pressure.
Low-volume/measurement artifact: refuted by consistent ~1.2s p50 across repeated windows at higher throughput (1.95 rps) and by the deterministic recovery to single-digit ms after removal.
